What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

These sides both want to play football and we can safely say (famous last words) that it won’t be 0-0 at 90 minutes.

Even by his prodigious standards, this has been a different week for Rio Ngumoha. After the coming-of-age performance against Villarreal, so followed the slew of attention on social media.

A clip of his best moments during the chaotic 4-3 dispatching of the Spaniards, posted on Uefa’s official X account, attracted 1.2 million views and was liked more than 24,000 times. Hot on the heels came another video, this time when he was 11, when he nutmegged a dumbfounded cameraman.

Ngumoha has always had feet that move as quickly as the hands of street artists who perform tricks with cups and balls: now you see it, now you don’t. We live in an age where talent is quickly amplified and this young England international has it in bundles.

You saw it in those exhilarating 74 minutes: Ngumoha had his most touches in a game this campaign (51), most touches in the opposition box (12) and attempted the most dribbles (10), as well as creating the most chances (three) and providing two assists.

It is the first time an 18-year-old has produced such figures in the Champions League since Opta’s European records began in 2008-09.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Liverpool and Brighton & Hove Albion at Anfield.

Liverpool are on a three-game winning run in all competitions, and came from two goals behind in their previous outing in the Champions League on Tuesday, earning an enthralling 4-3 victory over Villarreal. Last weekend, Andoni Iraola’s men also initially fell behind against Brentford in the Premier League, but netted two second-half goals through Daniel Munoz and Alexander Isak to win 2-1 as their opponents finished with nine men.

In his programme notes, Liverpool boss Iraola was excited about the prospect of a second game in a week at home. “As someone who believes every single opportunity we have to play a game at this stadium and in front of our supporters is a privilege, I also feel very passionately that this is a period that we should continue to embrace,” he said.

“It is also a spell in which we will carry on being tested because the quality of the opposition dictates that there is no chance of anything else. Fabian Hurzeler’s side sit third in the table, having scored a whopping 23 goals in their opening seven games, while conceding just five. #1347. Journey to Wembley: Halifax set sights on winning more fans and climbing mountain to the Football League as their FA Cup adventure is ended by route-one Cheltenham

By IAN HERBERT AT EV CHARGER POINTS STADIUM

Published: 21:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 18:05 EST, 9 November 2026

The FC Halifax manager John McGrath’s father-in-law is the top British mountaineer Alan Hinkes OBE and he knows that he has something of a summit of his own to scale, as he walks straight from the team bus to the pitch, set in the lee of Cheltenham’s mist-shrouded Cleeve Hill.

McGrath is all-too familiar with this setting. He brought his Buxton team here in the FA Cup's second round last season and was on the fringes of a major upset – 2-1 up at half-time – before watching the game fall away.

Cheltenham are a much stronger club, 12 months on, but our few weeks with McGrath, an Irishman who 25 years ago was playing for Aston Villa against Liverpool in the Premier League, reveal his ambition for the National League side he joined this summer.

We’re alongside him and FC Halifax on our journey to Wembley, told through all 13 rounds, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

A mist-veiled evening at Halifax’s Shay Stadium, a few weeks back, revealed much about 46-year-old McGrath. He arrives with his two-man coaching team for a Q&A with fans who, when the evening’s proceedings are finished, form a long and orderly queue to talk to him, one-on-one. The team’s four-hour drive to Southend awaits the following morning. But McGrath has no eye for the clock.

This managerial journey is one he hadn’t anticipated when, aged 32, a serious foot injury ended his long career with Burton Albion. He secured a master’s degree in broadcasting and media at Staffordshire University and had begun spots for Sky Sports and BBC local radio, yet here he is on ‘the grass’ he'd never wanted to leave.

His wife Fiona is Director of Public Realm at Islington Council and their time together is some weeks limited to a coffee at Doncaster station, near their home, when he drops her before daybreak. ‘It’s our little half an hour,’ he relates. ‘We’re ships that pass in the night.'

Cheltenham edged out FC Halifax 2-0 in front of 2,961 fans to reach round two

Cheltenham boss Steve Cotterill shakes hands with Halifax manager John McGrath

Ground staff put up the goalposts at EV Charger Points Stadium, also known as Whaddon Road

His club’s fans are partisan – 350 are here – and yearn for League Two, though there’s not a fortune at McGrath’s disposal. The club’s owner David Bosomworth was at the club when it went bust in 2008 and they say that experience left him painfully aware of the need for sustainability. Fair enough. Bosomworth has declined to speak to us. He is not at Cheltenham.

An hour out from kick-off, McGrath is handing out training vests for the warm-up as well as observing things – it’s a modest backroom team – and that defeat last season perhaps plays on his mind. ‘Cheltenham tweaked it that day and personally, I think I should have done the same,’ he says. ‘I’m a better manager, 12 months on.’

The club could badly use the £50,000 prize money that a win here would bring, not to mention the accompanying shot of exhilaration.

McGrath already belongs in the margins of the tournament’s history. He and his son, Jay, a Doncaster Rovers player, became the first father and son to play in the same team in an FA Cup game when McGrath, Mickleover Sports' player-manager for their preliminary-round win against Coventry Sphinx in 2019, fielded his 17-year-old boy.

Halifax seem up for this challenge. Their players go looking for their kit in their bus's luggage compartment before the driver has jumped out to produce the key. But Cheltenham have come a long way in the past year.

The former Burnley owner Mike Garlick bought the club 15 months ago and his investment strategy has echoes of the methods which made the Turf Moor club a Premier League side for seven out of eight years. Manager Steve Cotterill, quickly installed by Garlick, was briefly with him at Burnley.

Cheltenham fans arrive at the ground with their side riding high, fifth in League Two

Halifax fans cheer on their side but their Cup run is over - they travel to Kidderminster next Saturday in the National League

Mike Garlick bought Cheltenham last year and quickly installed Cotterill as manager

There’s an air of optimism around the place, as head groundsman Paul Gibson attends to some stray grass cuttings with a leaf blower and husband and wife team Gerry and Hannah Oldham sort the kit.

The ground staff, with their distinctive West Country burr, take enjoyment from several attempts at installing the goalposts before getting them upright. Mascot ‘Whaddney the Robin’ is limbering up for a leisurely lap of the stadium.

Garlick suggests we use Cotterill’s office as a quiet place to talk as the stadium begins to fill up. He tries calling the manager for his consent to do so but Cotterill’s phone rings out in the room.

It turns out Cotterill is receiving calls on his watch. This is a source of some humour as Cotterill eventually barrels into the office, exhibiting his usual energy. The two men clearly get on.

Extra preliminary round, August 8: Nelson 3-2 Stockport Georgians

Preliminary round, August 22: Witton Albion 1-0 Nelson

1st qualifying round, September 5: Avro 0-2 Witton Albion

2nd qualifying round, September 19: South Shields 7-0 Witton Albion

3rd qualifying round, October 3: Buxton 0-2 South Shields

4th qualifying round, October 17: Halifax 3-2 South Shields

1st round, November 7: Cheltenham Town 2-0 Halifax

Garlick looks more at home here than at Burnley. He also owns Spanish third-tier side Antequera CF and a club in Gibraltar but yearned for this kind of environment and Cheltenham, tumbling towards the EFL exit last year, badly needed help.

‘I missed English football,’ Garlick says. ‘I thought this was a club where I could make a difference and have some impact. When I came in, we had four points from nine games and were bottom of the league. It was hard work last season, but the fans seem happy for me to be here.

'Everyone who comes up to me says “thanks for helping the club,” which is nice. I never quite got that at Burnley to be honest. I’ve probably got more thanks here in 12 months than in 17 years on the board at Burnley. But that’s football isn’t it?!’

There’s been substantial investment in the training ground, a new stadium hospitality lounge, and Cotterill’s contacts have contributed to some eye-catching signings including veteran former Villa forward Andreas Weimann from Rapid Vienna.

Halifax start the game well, with wingers Ben Tollitt and Connor Douglas both flying and Conor Carty, the Irish forward who has been a revelation this season, ready to receive. Twice, they go close in the early stages. But Cotterill has a very uncomplicated route-one method in place and whip-fast striker Kirsten Otchere, on loan from Leicester City, looks lethal.

Will Flint’s string of fine interventions for Halifax is matched by the excellence of goalkeeper True Grant but Otchere crosses from the left for Jake Evans to score, left-footed.

This time McGrath does change things, adjusting the defensive line to quell Otchere’s threat after half time. Cotterill, whose colourful touchline antics include shoving his full-back out of the way when he blocks his line of view, grows concerned as Cheltenham’s attacking threat fades and Halifax dominate.

Carty nets from a Douglas’ crosses but is offside. Halifax lack the moment of class to convert superiority into goals. Substitute George Miller’s late header ended Halifax’s tournament for another year.

Halifax's Ben Tollitt battles for possession but his side cannot find a way through Cheltenham

McGrath and his Halifax players applaud the travelling supporters after their Cup exit

The Cheltenham fans flood out into suburban Whaddon Road fortified in their belief that something is building. ‘An FA Cup run is great for morale and also a massive contribution to the finances, because we’re hopefully going to strengthen again in January and the summer,’ says Garlick.

A foggy trip up the M6 awaits Halifax, though McGrath brings both a hinterland and perspective to the quest of start filling the famous old Shay Stadium once more and pushing closer to the fourth tier after 24 years away. His father-in-law was the first Briton to climb all the world's 8,000m mountains, in the Himalayan and Karakoram ranges of Nepal, Tibet and Pakistan.

‘He’s one of the best in the world,’ McGrath relates. ‘And however tough it is being a footballer or football manager, you try sitting on the side of Mount Everest for three months.

‘There’s a rumour building in our town that we play good football, that there’s goals to be seen at our stadium and a bunch of talented young men are representing the club in the right way.

'We want to get another 800 fans a week through the door and kick the club up the division and into the Football League. We think we can do that.’

READ MORE: Halifax reach first round in a beloved stadium they may soon lose

#1346. How a once-controversial idea is advancing understanding of Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Nuwer is a freelance writer based in New York City.

Microbiologist Sarkis Mazmanian says environmental factors often have a role in Parkinson’s.Credit: California Institute of Technology

Myriam Penninckx was having lunch at a restaurant in Brussels when her right arm began to shake. This was just the latest in a string of signs that something might be amiss. Her handwriting had suddenly become impossible to decipher, and she had noticed herself slowing down, physically and mentally. “I had always been Speedy Gonzales, doing a lot of things at the same time,” she says. “But that was becoming less possible.”

Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after her 60th birthday. She retired from her job and became depressed. “It was really hard to be someone who had a beautiful career, and then suddenly become a Parkinson’s patient,” she says. Her social life also ground to a halt. “If you have a tremor and you cannot cut your fish or eat your spaghetti, you don’t go out any more,” she says. “You close yourself to the world.”

When Penninckx heard about an unusual clinical trial being run at Ghent University in Belgium, she decided to enrol. In July 2021, she underwent a procedure that entailed flushing out her gut, and giving her a faecal transplant from a healthy donor to replace the community of microorganisms living there. The results, she says, “were amazing”. Her arm tremor went away and has not returned. She feels like the trial gave her “another shot at life”.

It might, at first, sound counterintuitive that such microbiome-targeting treatment could have marked benefits for people with Parkinson’s. Physicians have long been taught that the disease is a brain disorder that affects mainly the dopamine system, and that the hallmarks of the disease are Lewy bodies — misfolded clumps of a protein called α-synuclein that build up in neurons. But scientists have realized that the rest of the body is also involved, and the gut, in particular. For many individuals with Parkinson’s, evidence points to the gut’s involvement in the disease many years before diagnosis, says Per Borghammer, a neuroscientist at Aarhus University in Denmark.

Changes in the microbiome are also linked to some early symptoms and faster progression of the disease. These observations suggest that there are different subtypes of Parkinson’s, adds Filip Scheperjans, a neurologist at Helsinki University Hospital.

The gut’s seemingly central role in many Parkinson’s cases has implications not only for a better understanding of the disease’s origins and biology but also for tailoring treatments to an individual’s profile. “I make the comparison with what we see in oncology and cancer research,” says Arnout Bruggeman, the neurologist at Ghent University Hospital who oversaw Penninckx’s faecal transplant. Recognizing that various cancers exist as subtypes has allowed scientists to design vastly better treatments, he says — something he hopes will also be the case for Parkinson’s.

Hints that the gut is involved in Parkinson’s have been around since the disease was first described. People commonly have gastrointestinal issues, which sometimes start years before diagnosis. In 2003, researchers suggested that the α-synuclein pathology seen in the central nervous system might originate at peripheral sites, including the gut1. The work “introduced the idea that Parkinson’s disease starts very localized and then spreads via the neural connections”, Borghammer says. “It’s a little analogous to cancer that starts in one place and then metastasizes.”

Dozens of papers subsequently revealed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differ from those of people without the disease. In 2016, Sarkis Mazmanian, a microbiologist at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, showed that the microbiome plays a crucial part in the development of Parkinson’s-like symptoms in mice engineered to overexpress α-synuclein2. The animals’ symptoms went away when the researchers obliterated their microbiomes, and returned when they restored them. The team also transplanted human microbiomes into the mice, and found that rodents that received transplants from people with Parkinson’s had worse symptoms than did those who received transplants from healthy people.

In 2019, Borghammer and his colleague proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into two main subtypes, according to where α-synuclein originates3. The ‘brain first’ subtype of the disease, he says, starts in the olfactory bulb, whereas a ‘body first’ version starts in the gut. This idea was controversial at first, and some researchers are still sceptical. But after years of mounting evidence, most are coming around to the idea.

Body-first Parkinson’s is thought to progress faster, and often manifests first with disturbances to the REM stage of sleep, gastrointestinal issues, depression, loss of smell and damage to the nerves that supply the heart (see ‘Teasing out distinct origins’). Brain-first Parkinson’s, by contrast, usually begins with motor symptoms. Eventually the subtypes converge — the end stage of the disease is the same, Borghammer says, it just starts in different places.

Source: P. Borghammer J. Neural Transm. 130, 737–753 (2023).

For both brain-first and body-first subtypes, the majority of Parkinson’s cases are attributable to “something you came across in your life”, Mazmanian says. Environmental risk factors seem to include air pollution, heavy metals, pesticides, certain viral infections and possibly microplastics.

Genes also play a part, however, and there is no bright-line distinction between genetic and environmental causes; the two are often linked. Variants of a gene called GBA1 are most closely associated with body-first Parkinson’s. But only a minority of carriers of the gene actually develop the disease, leading researchers to wonder what external factors might also have a role.

A study in April explored the part that the microbiome might play in increasing that risk, by examining hundreds of participants in the United Kingdom and Italy who did and did not have Parkinson’s, and likewise did and did not have a GBA1 variant linked to the disease4. The researchers analysed the participants’ stool samples and confirmed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differed significantly from those of people without the disease, and that the more severe the participant’s disease, the more altered was their microbiome. Mirroring earlier findings in mice, they also confirmed that, regardless of whether they carried a variant, people with Parkinson’s had roughly the same altered microbiome. This suggests that the disease process does more to transform a gut microbiome than do a person’s genes, says Elisa Menozzi, a clinical neuroscientist now at Aarhus University, and a co-author of the study.

As they had expected, Menozzi and her colleagues also found that healthy people carrying a GBA1 variant had, on average, microbiomes shifted toward the Parkinson’s pattern. But given that both carriers and non-carriers who already had Parkinson’s had statistically indistinguishable microbiomes, it seems that the variant itself is not what drives this change. Furthermore, in healthy participants not every carrier had this microbiome shift, and carriers who showed early, subtle signs of disease had microbiomes that looked most like those of people with Parkinson’s. Roughly one in five healthy participants without the variant also had the same altered microbiomes and signs that could be early markers of disease. The researchers’ interpretation, Menozzi says, is that changes to the microbiome raise the risk of Parkinson’s independently of genetics.

Taken together, Menozzi says, the findings suggest that the microbiome could be a diagnostic marker of Parkinson’s before symptoms become noticeable. Confirming this will require following the participants over time to see whether any of them develop Parkinson’s — something the team is doing, says co-author Anthony Schapira, a neurologist at University College London.

Although the study did not address what is causing the microbiome to change, the researchers found a significant association with participants’ eating habits. Diets that were high in vegetables, fruits and polyunsaturated fats seemed to protect against a Parkinson’s-type microbiome, whereas those high in saturated fat and low in fibre were associated with a microbiome closer to that of someone with the disease-altered microbiome. So dietary intervention is worth investigating, Schapira says. “The first question to answer is, can you do anything about this — can you change the microbiome?” he says. “ The next question is, does it matter?”

Some evidence from human trials already indicates that harnessing the microbiome to treat Parkinson’s could be possible. When Penninckx told her family that she would be receiving a faecal transplant as part of a study, she encountered some scepticism. “My grandchildren said, ‘Are you going to eat it?’” she recalls. She was relieved that was not the case. Instead, the researchers inserted a plastic tube into her nose, snaking it through her stomach and into her small intestine. “You’re never in contact with the material, so it’s not like there is a bad smell or taste,” she says.

Penninckx was one of 22 participants in the 2024 study to receive a faecal transplant from a healthy donor, while another 24 people were given a placebo made up of their own gut flora5. Twelve months after treatment, those who received the active treatment had fewer motor symptoms and less constipation than did those in the control group. The researchers plan to launch a larger trial this autumn to replicate these findings, Bruggeman says. Future trials will also analyse the composition of the microbiomes of healthy donors, which he says is “a key question” for determining the source of a potential positive effect.

Per Borghammer proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into subtypes.Credit: Tonny Foghmar

Not all the results have been this promising. Scheperjans and his colleagues did not see a significant improvement in 30 participants who received an active treatment in a double-blind, placebo-controlled faecal transplant trial6. They do not know why their results differed from those in Belgium, but they suspect it might have had something to do with the method of delivery. The team administered treatment into the colon of participants rather than into the small intestine, which contains more immune cells than the large intestine. “It may be that for immune-system regulation, the small bowel is more important,” he says.

Surprisingly, the placebo group in this trial experienced more benefits than did the active treatment group. Up to 12 months after treatment, those in the placebo group had less constipation and more relief of some motor symptoms, as well as more changes to their microbiomes. The researchers think that this might be related to the bowel cleansing that all participants underwent before treatment — a hypothesis that they plan to test in a follow-up study. “If you have an abnormal microbiome, maybe the bowel cleansing gives you an opportunity to get recolonized with more normal bacteria,” Scheperjans says. “We’ll know if that’s the case after the next trial.”

Borghammer suspects that the differing faecal transplant results might come down to how “incredibly crude” the trials so far have been, simply because the field is so new. For example, researchers do not yet have the knowledge that would allow them to select the best donors for participants. Given this, he does not think that inconclusive results should be discouraging. “It’s plausible that it can work,” he says. “We just don’t understand it well enough yet.”

Another potential problem for faecal-transplant trials — and for research on Parkinson’s interventions in general — is that studies usually lump together people with body-first and brain-first subtypes. This could be confounding the results, Borghammer says, because different forms of the disease are likely to be driven by different mechanistic pathways. In 2022, for example, a phase III trial of an immunotherapy treatment targeting α-synuclein failed to produce significant results. But when the researchers later analysed the data for participants only with the most severe Parkinson’s, they found that the treatment did seem to slow progression of motor symptoms7. “It looks like for the fast-progressing type, which is strongly associated with the body-first type, it might have actually worked,” Borghammer says. “But because the original study included a mixed group of unselected patients, the clinical trial might have been unable to show statistically significant results.”

Myriam Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after turning 60.Credit: Courtesy of Myriam Penninckx

Researchers are increasingly aware of these limitations, and some groups are looking more closely at the bacterial species and mechanisms involved — and at more targeted populations. Haydeh Payami, a geneticist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, and her team found that the gut microbiomes of about one-quarter of people with Parkinson’s contain high levels of a protein that induces aggregation of α-synuclein8. That protein is produced only by the bacterium Escherichia coli, giving scientists “one defined target”, says Mazmanian, who collaborates with Payami. Vertero Therapeutics, a firm Mazmanian co-founded in Woburn, Massachusetts, have developed a drug that inhibits production of the E. coli protein, and in mice it prevented α-synuclein from aggregating. “You can just stop this process in its tracks,” Mazmanian says.

In May, Vertero began a phase I trial in people with Parkinson’s whose microbiome matches the bacterial profile targeted by the drug. “In the population that we can treat, our hope is to slow down or even stop Parkinson’s progression,” Mazmanian says. “That would be a huge victory.”

The ultimate goal, however, is to be able to identify people in the very early stages of the disease, and then use pharmaceuticals, faecal transplants, dietary changes or other interventions to alter their trajectory. “Fast forward a decade, I hope we’ll be able to treat people before they actually develop Parkinson’s,” Mazmanian says.

Five years on, Penninckx still feels empowered by the gains she experienced in the faecal-transplant trial. She keeps busy as a board member of Parkili, a Belgian charity that supports scientific research — including some of Bruggeman’s work — and arranges trips around the world for people with Parkinson’s. She has travelled to Jordan with the group, and in May, she and seven others represented it at the World Parkinson’s Conference in Phoenix, Arizona. “I’ve started a new life,” she says. “So my story is a happy one.”

Penninckx knows that her disease is not cured. But her experience hints at the potential benefits that the mounting appreciation of the Parkinson’s gut–brain connection could bring.

#1344. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another important save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo

Had the former Newcastle United player scored so late in the game, the home crowd’s frustration may have boiled over. The point means Le Bris’ side have still not won a league game since August and remain bottom of the table. This is proving to be a tougher second season in the top flight for Sunderland, but if they keep playing like this, they will not remain in the bottom three for much longer.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

“It’s still a long journey, we know with this busy schedule playing in Europe, playing in the Carabao Cup, it’s a new challenge for us and we need to embrace it. I think we showed this afternoon that we are in this challenge, we want to embrace it and be ourselves and we probably deserved a bit more today.”

75.8% - The combined pass completion rate from today's @premierleague matches was just 75.8%. This is the lowest on a single day with 5+ matches played since 14th December 2019 (75.1%). 🌪️ Boelo. https://t.co/34WdKllPCH

"On another day we win" James Trafford assesses Leeds' 0-0 draw with Sunderland 🗣️ https://t.co/CZpftPCJSp

James Trafford speaks on his start to life at Leeds after another clean sheet 👏 https://t.co/E9wrzdheAD

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Sunderland man said: “I think the wind played a big part and credit to both defences and the attacks as well to be able to keep it to no goals in that swirling wind.

“I think it was a good effort from everybody so obviously we want three points from where we are in the table but keep putting up the performances like that and we’ll get some.

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

“It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some big saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”

When asked about Sunderland being bottom of the league, he replied: “I think always the table reflects fairly where teams deserve to be, and I think over the course of the course of the season if we keep putting in performances like that it will represent where we should be.

“But the table always reflects where people should be but we need to keep looking at ourselves, don’t look at other anyone else, it’s no-one else’s fault but us and we know that.”

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

Full-time from the Stadium of Light as the points are shared between Sunderland and Leeds 🤝 https://t.co/ij9ioYEJH5

Ampadu’s cross finds its way to Okafor, who helps the ball into the danger zone towards Longstaff. The midfielder shoots from close range, but Sunderland throw in a couple of bodies to block it.

Talbi dreadfully overhits a corner straight out of play for a goal kick... that sums this game up.

Former Newcastle United midfielder Longstaff gallops forward and fires a low effort towards goal, but Roefs makes a great stop to tip the strike around the post for a corner. That was substitute’s first involvement after entering the action. Think it’s safe to say he wouldn’t be a popular scorer given his previous ties to Sunderland’s bitter rivals. There will be six minutes of added time.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another important save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo

There’s a straight swap in Leeds’ midfield as Tanaka is withdrawn for Longstaff. This game appears destined to be 0-0. Can either side find a late winner?

Leeds make the next change as Nmecha replaces Calvert-Lewin up top. Trafford collides with Muharemovic as he comes out to claim a cross. He initially stays down and it looks like he has cramp, but he’s okay to continue and play resumes.

There are appeals for a penalty as Tutierov’s deflected cross hits Tanaka’s shoulder. It’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

It is rare you watch a game of football for more than an hour and cannot say with clarity who has been the better of the two sides. Sunderland have had their moments and Leeds’ James Trafford has been the busier of the two. Yet, Leeds have also had periods in the game when they have looked the more threatening and it has taken some valiant last ditch defending from the home side to deny them.

There’s a double change for Sunderland as Diarra and Talbi replace Angulo and Le Fee. Can either of these substitutes help the hosts claim a victory?

A double change from RLB 🔄 https://t.co/8E2MVJYLyM

On the turn, Tanaka swivels and shoots from just outside the penalty area. Roefs spills the fierce strike and Calvert-Lewin attempts to pounce on to the rebound. The goalkeeper gets another hand to the ball, preventing the striker from a tap-in. There are cries from the Leeds support up high in the away end for a penalty, but the situation is quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Robin Roefs produced a quick double save to deny Tanaka and Calvert-Lewin from opening the scoring for Leeds 🧤 https://t.co/9otOjISuNh

Bogle bursts forward on the right flank and fires a powerful, teasing cross towards the back post. Okafor makes the run, but Sadiki is there to make a terrific interception and clear the danger.

Sunderland take advantage of the windy conditions as Trafford flaps at Xhaka’s looped corner. The ball drops to Angulo, whose low, driven half-volley is blocked by a sea of Leeds bodies.

Le Fee tries to slide an intricate pass through to Tutierov, but it’s cut out by Bijol, who reads the situation well.

Bogle catches Reinildo above his hip with a high boot. The referee gives the Leeds man a yellow card. Sunderland want something more. That was certainly a risky tackle from Bogle, who now must be careful.

Let's go, Timur 👊 https://t.co/JVxgPM7zAC

Attacking changes are here for both sides. Brobbey’s Sunderland return lasts for over an hour and he’s replaced by Tutierov. Meanwhile, for the visitors, Wilson and Aaronson depart for Stach and Okafor.

Bogle carelessly catches Angulo with a late tackle, gifting Sunderland a great chance to swing the ball into the box. Le Fee whips it in, but its flicked on and goes out for a goal kick.

This game is now being played at a much quicker tempo, with Justin bending an effort towards the far top corner. However, it drifts wide. Both sides look far more confident now and not like they’re playing for a draw.

At the other end, the ball breaks to Angulo, who stings Trafford’s palms with a fierce curling strike that forces the Leeds goalkeeper into conceding a corner. Excitement in this second half is starting to ramp up.

Leeds come forward again as Bogle tries to slide a low cross into Tanaka, but Le Fee tracks back to prevent the visitors from getting a shot off.

Wilson whips in a deep corner. Muharemovic wins the header at the back stick, but can’t get threatening contact on it and slowly directs it into Roefs’ grasp.

If I’m being kind to the players out there, playing in a strong wind at the Stadium of Light is notoriously tricky.

If you are watching on television, you might have noticed in the first half the litter being blown around in circles on the pitch. That will give you an idea of the conditions. The wind tends to swirl around inside this stadium rather than blowing in one direction. If I were any good at physics I would be able to tell you why. But I’m not. So I can’t.

Still, this match is yet to strike an attacking rhythm. Leeds have dominated the ball since the break, with Mukiele’s injury and subsequent departure slightly unsettling the hosts. Aaronson acrobatically knocks the ball across the six-yard box, but it’s hooked clear by Sunderland.

Mukiele won’t return to the action and heads down the tunnel. Alderete is on to replace his fellow defender. That is a blow for Sunderland to lose Mukiele this early in the second half.

We're forced into a change 🔄 https://t.co/ZJB0NOnawt

Mukiele is sat up and is still receiving treatment after being caught by O’Nein on his Adam’s apple. He walks off the pitch and it’s unclear if he’s able to continue. For now, Sunderland are down to 10 men.

The medical staff are waved on to the pitch as O’Nein accidentally catches Mukiele in the face with his outstretched arm.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Only two shots on target in that first half, with Brobbey forcing a couple of saves from Trafford. Hopefully we’re treated to some more exciting football after the break.

In a game lacking creativity and chances, nothing separates Sunderland and Leeds at the break. The best chance of the first half fell to Brobbey, but Trafford did well to smother the one-on-one opportunity.

There will be just one minute of added time to end this first half.

Nearly a disaster at the back for Sunderland as O’Nein lets a ball run thinking Roefs will come out to clear. However, the goalkeeper stays put. With Calvert-Lewin closing in, O’Nein has to make a last-ditch sliding challenge to direct the ball back to Roefs to stop the striker in his tracks.

Reinildo is booked as Bogle turns him, with the Sunderland defender dragging the Leeds man to the florr. He protests his innocence, and in fairness to Reinildo, he has a ripped shirt. He must be freezing.

Hume draws huge applause from the home fans as he crunches into a challenge on Gudmundsson. The Sunderland fans loved that sliding tackle.

Leeds are still waiting to record a shot on target. They’ve been pretty safe and unadventurous in forward areas so far.

A lot of huff and puff, honest endeavour and robust challenges in this game so far, but the two moments of quality have come from Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. His first save to deny Brian Brobbey was excellent. He perfectly judged the trajectory of an awkward bouncing ball at full stretch, but I think the second is even better.

Trafford was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international but the way he stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb. He may have saved with his feet, but he cramped Brobbey for room and timed his moment to dive at his feet perfectly. That was elite level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Ampadu picks up the game’s first yellow card for bumping into Angulo on the edge of his own box. Sunderland now have a free kick in a promising position. Unfortunately for the hosts, Le Fee smacks it straight into the wall.

Sunderland’s pressure nearly pays off as Xhaka forces Wilson into a mistake. Brobbey is then too strong for Bijol and shrugs the defender off the ball. From a tight angle, the striker has a one-on-one opportunity against Trafford, but the Leeds goalkeeper does well to block Brobbey’s side-footed effort.

Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

On his return to the Sunderland line-up, Brobbey tests Trafford in Sunderland’s first attack. The striker’s deflected effort bounces awkwardly in front of the goalkeeper, who parries the ball out for a corner. Leeds then defend the set-piece well and clear the danger.

That was a deceptively hard save for James Trafford to make to deny Brian Brobbey. Although the connection was not the cleanest, that almost made it harder as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the England international meant he had to watch it all the way and keep a strong hand at full stretch. Excellent work from the summer signing from Manchester City.

Leeds are dominating the ball in these early exchanges. Sunderland look slightly unsettled so far. Bogle is pushing particularly far forward for the visitors.

Wilson starts for Leeds. The Welshman was pivotal for Fulham last season. His Leeds career is yet to meaningfully get going, but he has a great chance to impress today.

Leeds get us under way here. How will come out on top in these feisty northern weather conditions?

My favourite part of every Sunderland game is the singing of Elvis Presley’ Can’t Help Falling in Love before kick off. Not sure the “The King” had a football club on Wearside in mind when he wrote it but it just works as a pre-match anthem. I also grew up in a house where there was a lot of Elivs playing when I was a small child. Anyway, on to the football.

The Stadium of Light is in fantastic spirits as per usual, despite Sunderland floundering in 20th position. Can the home side record a much-needed win to ignite their domestic season?

Starting good in the season, we are really keen to follow our goals for our system where we train every week and we follow how our team should play.

And, how the XI plus the subs should play together, fight for each other, and we have to keep on going like this. We know how good Sunderland are.

The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1343. 'I've never revealed the whole story': England fans wouldn't boo me if they knew the truth, says Ben White... as he defends World Cup walkout and rejecting call-ups

Published: 15:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 18:20 EST, 9 November 2026

Ben White believes England fans would not boo him if they knew the truth behind his 2022 World Cup walkout.

The Arsenal defender left the camp in Qatar after the group stages citing 'personal reasons', although a fallout with Gareth Southgate's assistant, Steve Holland, was later reported. He then declined a return to the England set-up while Southgate and Holland were in charge but was included by Thomas Tuchel in March of this year.

However, White was booed by fans inside Wembley when he came on in the second-half of a friendly against Uruguay, only to score his first international goal and then concede a late penalty in a 1-1 draw. He was not selected for the World Cup in North America but is back with the squad ahead of this week's Nations League fixtures against Croatia and Spain.

And the 29-year-old, addressing those jeers for the first time, said: 'It was hard to hear, especially because they didn't know the situation, which is kind of what I put my mind to.

'They don't know my situation and it is not really about what I have done, because they don't know why, and if they did they would not be booing or saying these things. I just think about maybe (them) not knowing the full story, and if they did, maybe they wouldn't (boo).'

He added: 'Obviously, a load has been said. I've probably seen all of it. I just think people don't know the full story, because I've never said anything, and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

Ben White has insisted he would not be booed by England fans if they knew the truth behind his World Cup walkout

White fell out with former England assistant Steve Holland (left) before heading home during the 2022 World Cup

'There were loads of things that happened and communication wasn't great. I don't want to throw anyone under the bus. A lot of people try to do that to me so it's something I wouldn't want to do myself. I think it's probably the best way. It's a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it's amazing to be here now. It's a privilege to be called up.'

White, however, is adamant that he would make the same decision today and leave the World Cup, even if he will not divulge the reasons as to why.

'I don't think I would (do anything different),' he said. 'I think, as a person, I'm quite real, and I made the decision that I would probably continue to make. It's one that I'm not happy about. It wasn't ideal. But it happened, it's time to move on.

'I don't think I am looking to win anyone over or say anything that helps them get back on my side. It is what it is. There are reasons for it and I am just looking forward to playing for England and doing well and looking for success.'

White has spoken publicly about not watching football, and this, too, has been used against him by some supporters.

'It doesn't mean I don't like football, because I do it every day, so I must like it a little bit!' he said. 'It's because I don't watch it, which I think is quite normal for someone that does a job and then doesn't go home and then continue watching that job.

'I don't think anyone knows my personality. I keep that to my loved ones and family. It's all noise when people have an opinion on that stuff. It is not actually me. People don't know me and I like it that way. You give so much to the game, which is intense. I think it's important to keep some bits for yourself. I keep the energy for the people I love.'

England new boy Josh King believes his aptitude for academia gives him an advantage at the start of a burgeoning career.

The Fulham star – who has two Premier League goals this season – linked up with Thomas Tuchel’s squad on Monday morning as one of two fresh call ups alongside Jobe Bellingham.

King was a straight-A student at the renowned independent Hampton School in south London, with alumni including Queen guitarist Sir Brian May and golf pro Paul Casey.

The teenager’s mother, Michelle, is a university lecturer and finishing a PhD on sickle cell disease while his father Steve is a personal injury lawyer.

‘The most important thing about being good academically and education-wise is you’re able to take on information much more quickly,’ King said.

‘You can take on information which might take a bit longer for other people. I think that definitely helps.’

While the 19-year-old was invited to take part in a pre-World Cup training camp in Miami, he is hoping to make his international bow against Croatia on Thursday.

Although a central figure in Fulham’s midfield, a confident King could be utilised wider by Tuchel were he to be given an opportunity across the two-game Nations League camp.

‘There was a buzz around Fulham when I got called up [this week],’ he added. ‘I got off the phone with the boss, ran into the kitchen and started cheering with my dad. I called mum at work and she was screaming in the office. This felt slightly unachievable when I was younger.’

Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were namechecked as those who helped him settle when introduced to the group in Florida, with King having also studied the likes of Jamal Musiala and Pedri to elevate his own game.

‘The main thing you take is the standards they set,’ he said when reflecting on joining the camp in America. ‘The way they conduct themselves, the way they perform every day, the way they train and the way they take everything seriously.

‘The little things, technical things, the way some people strike the ball, the way some people pass, just little things which you almost take without thinking about it - they also have an impact.

‘On a few occasions I asked “how do you finish this way” or “what do you do in this scenario” and it always helps to add to my game.’

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections swept the Democratic party to power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump.

The results will mark the end of nearly two years in which the Republicans controlled the presidency and both congressional chambers — and many scientists around the world are celebrating the change as an opportunity to protect the country’s research system.

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

“This is a big win,” says Megan Peters, a cognitive scientist who moved in 2025 from the University of California, Irvine, to University College London, in part because of worries about US science. “It’s a demonstration that US [voters] are dissatisfied with what the current administration has been doing.” Scientific research, she adds, “is America’s superpower, and it’s been cut at the knees”.

Those hopeful for change include researchers affected by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) being shut down early in Trump’s presidency. “I’m cautiously optimistic,” says Quarraisha Abdool Karim, an epidemiologist at the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, which is headquartered in Durban and had partnered with USAID on clinical trials. “What we’ve seen in the past 24 hours is that democracy and democratic principles, with individuals turning out to vote, can make a huge difference.” But, she adds, “we will not see overnight changes”.

As of 2.15 p.m. EST on 4 November, Democrats had secured at least 237 seats in the 435-seat US House of Representatives and 54 seats in the 100-member US Senate, giving them decisive majorities in both, with votes still being counted in some states. These majorities will give them the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda, although there will still be obstacles. For instance, given that Democrats haven’t won two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of Congress, the president can veto those bills.

Trump initially told The New York Times that he would accept the mid-term election results and that he would “look forward” to working with Democrats. Later, however, he posted an image of a red hat with the word ‘VETO’ on it to Truth Social, his social-media platform.

Since Donald Trump became president for the second time in January 2025, his administration has pushed for unprecedented cuts to science funding, politicized decision-making at federal science agencies and interfered with policies at US universities that receive federal funding.

When Democrats take charge of both chambers of the US Congress on 3 January 2027, they will be able to control congressional committees, including science committees; set agendas for hearings that investigate government officials and their science policies; and use legally binding subpoenas to compel the Trump administration to provide documents and testify in front of Congress.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

On social media, Democrats promised to make use of that authority. Robert Garcia, a representative from California who will soon chair the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, shared a two-word statement aimed at the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.” In particular, some scientists are calling for scrutiny of Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who has drafted a plan that gives political appointees, rather than scientist peer reviewers, control of decisions about research grants, and who has delayed the distribution of congressionally approved science funds.

Scientists and policy specialists said they were hoping to see more congressional oversight of the actions of Robert F. Kennedy Jr, the head of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), who has questioned vaccine safety, and whose tenure has coincided with the country’s worst measles resurgence in decades. “For sure, secretary Kennedy will be put on the hot seat” to explain his unscientific actions, says Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association in Washington DC. “What I’m hoping is that Congress will really push this administration to have a much more proactive response to the measles epidemic.”

Zoe Lofgren, a Democratic representative from California, said she would campaign to become the head of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees agencies such as NASA and the US National Science Foundation. “We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise,” she said in a statement.

Stand Up for Science, a science-advocacy group based in Atlanta, Georgia, that has organized protests against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science, says that it will release a plan on 5 November with strategies to push Congress for change.

Whether Congress will be able to increase funding for federal science, rather than just hold it relatively steady as they have for the past two years, is doubtful, however. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had protected science budgets, but she lost her re-election bid in these mid-terms. Large boosts to science spending could also just be difficult to pass, given that the budget must also be signed by Trump, who has tried to slash non-defence science spending.

Tottenham Hotspur are expected to make another significant investment in their attacking department during the January transfer window, with David Ornstein providing an encouraging update on the club’s pursuit of a new striker.

The north London club have struggled to find consistent goals from their centre-forwards this season, and Roberto De Zerbi is keen to address the problem as he looks to strengthen his squad.

Journalist David Ornstein believes Tottenham could make a major striker move in January, provided the right opportunity becomes available.

Speaking on The Athletic FC, he said: “I think in an ideal world, the best case scenario would be to sign a new striker who can be their line leader for the next 10 years.

“What we’ve seen of their ownership in recent times and their hierarchy is that they’re prepared to go big in the market and invest heavily and back Roberto De Zerbi.

“Their ambition is high, so if there were the perfect candidate on the market, I don’t have reason to think they wouldn’t go for them.”

Tottenham and Newcastle track 24-year-old Belgian ahead of potential transfer battle

The lack of reliable goalscoring options has become a growing concern for Spurs, with Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush failing to make the desired impact in the final third.

Tottenham have managed just 10 goals in their opening 10 Premier League matches, with only two coming from recognised strikers. Their attacking struggles were especially evident in their recent defeat against Leeds United.

Speaking on The Athletic FC podcast, Ornstein suggested that Tottenham’s hierarchy are willing to commit substantial funds to strengthen the position.

The journalist said the club’s ambitions remain high and that their willingness to back De Zerbi financially could matter if an outstanding candidate emerges.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Meanwhile, securing a quality centre-forward mid-season could prove challenging for Tottenham.

Several clubs across Europe are reluctant to part ways with their most important attacking players in January, making negotiations particularly complicated.

Bournemouth youngster Eli Junior Kroupi has previously attracted Spurs’ interest, but convincing the Cherries to sanction his departure could be difficult. Gustavo Varela and Younes Ebnoutalib are among the other forwards who could emerge as alternatives.

Tottenham will need to identify the right profile rather than simply add another attacking option to their squad. A proven goalscorer capable of leading the line could make a significant difference to De Zerbi’s side during the second half of the campaign.

#1340. Journaling, no days off and 'Mamba Mentality': How Senne Lammens is trying to arrest his slide in form - and why his Man United team-mates must take the blame for his shattered confidence

Published: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026

Senne Lammens will have gone home on Sunday night, picked up his journal and tried to make sense of where it all went horribly wrong.

Journaling is what keeps Lammens’ mind at ease and what allows him to move on from moments of disappointment, of which Sunday afternoon against Aston Villa will have ranked high on his list.

Lammens may have lamented his decision to use his knees, rather than his hands, in attempting to deal with Alysson’s strike in the first minute. And that he parried a shot straight to Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 three minutes later. Lammens is big on accountability. Nobody will have needed to tell him that he could have done much better.

The responsibility for Villa goals three and four, however, lands squarely at the feet of his team-mates, a familiar pattern across the season so far.

Still, this was Lammens' worst performance in a Manchester United shirt, and the player himself is unlikely to have come to a different conclusion. But he has not become a bad goalkeeper overnight. Far from it.

While there was plenty of attention on his two costly mistakes against Villa, many have seemingly forgotten about a crucial one-on-one save Lammens made to deny Julio Enciso in the opening home match against Ipswich Town. It was 0-0 then and United would go on to win 5-2.

Senne Lammens has had a difficult start to the season - and was partly at fault for two of the goals Manchester United conceded in Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

They have forgotten two brilliant saves he made at Fulham to deny Sander Berge, and then Josh King. The second, with his right foot, was sublime and kept a listing United in the game at 0-0.

Even in United's season opener, the 24-year-old did tremendously well to push Oli McBurnie’s goalbound effort onto the post, only for three of his back four to switch off, allowing Hull City to score en route to a 2-0 win.

Overlooked are the failed defensive assignments of Bryan Mbeumo (against Ipswich Town), or Carlos Baleba (against Leeds United), or the costly mistakes of Lisandro Martinez, Diogo Dalot and Leny Yoro.

Lammens’ own form has regressed, there’s no doubt about that, but no goalkeeper in the Premier League is being sold short by those in front of him more than the United No 1 right now.

Across 10 Premier League matches, no goalkeeper has faced more shots on his goal than Lammens (52), tied in first place with Newcastle United’s Lukas Hornicek.

It’s also worth noting that no goalkeeper has made more saves in a single Premier League match this season than Lammens’ eight at Chelsea. United went on to lose 2-0 that day.

Lammens has made the fourth-most saves this season and yet has conceded a league-high 19 goals (Crystal Palace's 24 have been let in by both Walter Benitez and Dean Henderson).

Last season, across 32 games, Lammens faced 118 shots, averaging 3.69 per game. Fast forward to this campaign and it’s 52 shots in 10 games, up to 5.2 per game, a stark increase in workload.

Only twice last season did Lammens face six or more shots in a Premier League game. This season it has happened four times already.

Lammens had a rush of the blood to the head when he came out – and missed out – as Evanilson knocked the ball past him to score Bournemouth’s third at Old Trafford last month

Mistakes, such as those at Everton, Fulham and at home to Villa, are costly. His distribution, too, has become a sore spot with Lammens ranking 15th of 16 ever-present goalkeepers for completed long passes (37 of 115 attempted).

But Lammens performed well in the last international break for Belgium behind competent defenders. He doesn’t have that luxury at United right now.

‘Sometimes in the end it comes down to maybe here and there, maybe a mistake from someone, but it doesn’t really start with that,’ Lammens said of United's defensive issues earlier this season.

‘I think it’s a team thing. The manager has been hammering a lot about defending as a team, being able to put pressure on the opposition team, especially on crosses.’

A key selling point for Lammens last season was the composure he brought and the calmness he exuded. He was everything to United that Andre Onana wasn’t. That’s been chipped away this season.

A nervousness has crept in. The misplaced pass against Tottenham Hotspur to Kobbie Mainoo that was never on, which saw him redeem himself with a strong save from Dominic Solanke. The rush of blood to come out – and miss out – as Evanilson knocked the ball past him to score Bournemouth’s third at Old Trafford. The judgment call to use his legs as the ball ricocheted off Martinez and into his own net at Fulham.

All of which has led to a pundit and social media pile-on of a goalkeeper that, in the eyes of some, is now out of his depth.

Which is where the journaling comes in. It helps Lammens' belief that things will turn for the better, and the composure of a man who didn’t get too high when he was anointed the Signing of the Season for 2025-26 across the entire Premier League, and who isn’t getting too low about the most scrutinised run of his career.

‘Especially at big clubs, you don't want a keeper who performs well one match and poorly the next,’ Lammens said back in September.

‘You want someone who is a rock behind the defence. Someone the team can rely on. That's definitely a major goal for me. It's something to embody as a goalkeeper.

‘You can compare it a bit to Edwin van der Sar. He's someone I admire greatly. What I want to take from his game is that calmness.’

Lammens' confidence was rocked by a mistake he made in Belgium's World Cup exit to Spain - and United's leaky defence has left him unable to build it back up

The 24-year-old is known to pass up days off to put in extra work, and sources say he is first in in the morning and last to head home at the end of training

Lammens is known to pass up days off to put in extra work, and sources say he is first in in the morning and last to head home at the end of training. There are even figures at United who believe parts of his game have improved on last season.

His confidence was rocked in the summer when his spill to Mikel Merino sent Belgium home from the World Cup and he has had little chance to build back that confidence given the storm back in Manchester.

Basketball legend Kobe Bryant is Lammens' idol. He sports the late LA Lakers star's numbers on his gloves and swears by his 'Mamba Mentality'. And if that mentality tells us anything, it’s that resilience and fearlessness win out.

Lammens is struggling but he’s still the same goalkeeper that was being lauded last season. He just needs a helping hand from those in front of him or this defence will be stuck in a never-ending cycle of misery.
